strengths: The paper tackles an important and challenging problem in self-supervised learning: how to generate effective data augmentations for general/non-vision modalities where intuitive, domain-specific geometric and photometric transformations are not readily available.

Extensive empirical evaluations are conducted across multiple non-vision benchmarks (HAR, Reuters, Epsilon, MSLR-WEB30K) and vision datasets (CIFAR-10/100, STL-10, ImageNet) across several base architectures (SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, SimSiam, DINO).

The qualitative visualizations (Figures 1, 4, 6, and 7) provide an interesting observation: learning input noise variance appears to place larger variance on background regions while preserving foreground object outlines.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification linking contrastive learning to Positive-incentive Noise (Pi-Noise) is tautological. The paper defines an auxiliary scalar random variable $\alpha | x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \gamma_{\theta^*}(x)^{-1})$ where $\gamma_{\theta^*}(x) = \exp(-\ell(x; \theta^*))$. Because the differential entropy of this Gaussian distribution is linearly related to $\log \gamma^{-1} = \ell(x; \theta^*)$, minimizing the conditional task entropy simply recovers the contrastive loss by mathematical construction. Rather than uncovering a genuine information-theoretic principle, the auxiliary variable is engineered specifically to yield the target objective.

The conceptual characterization of standard data augmentation as a 'point estimation of $\pi$-noise' via a Dirac delta distribution $p(\varepsilon|x) \to \delta_{\varepsilon_0}(\varepsilon)$ (Eq. 12) is fundamentally flawed. Standard visual augmentations (random cropping, rotations, color jitter) are stochastic policies over continuous or discrete transformation spaces, not a single deterministic point estimate $\varepsilon_0$.

There is an inherent objective conflict / shortcut problem when jointly minimizing Eq. (17) with respect to both the model parameters $\theta$ and the generator parameters $\psi$. If $\psi$ simply minimizes the contrastive loss, the generator is incentivized to produce trivial perturbations (e.g., near-zero noise) that make positive pairs identical and easiest to align. The paper mentions in Appendix B.4 that an ad-hoc penalty (the multiplicative inverse of the average norm of the noise) was added on vision datasets to keep the noise from collapsing to zero. This critical regularizer is omitted from the main text and formulation, indicating that the core objective alone does not naturally govern the trade-off.

The computational overhead is substantial without commensurate performance gains. As shown in Tables 6 and 9, training the noise generator (e.g., using a ResNet-18 generator alongside a ResNet-18 encoder) roughly doubles the training time, FLOPs, and GPU memory footprint. In standard visual settings with default augmentations (Table 3), the performance gains from adding PiNDA are often marginal (e.g., CIFAR-10 SR improves from 91.98% to 92.25% or 90.50%; CIFAR-100 SR from 70.43% to 70.64%).

The manuscript contains notable presentation and formatting defects, including unfinished placeholder sentences in the Abstract ('Our code is available at .') and Section 4.2 ('The source codes are available at .'), missing citations/formatting artifacts, and frequent grammatical errors throughout the text.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in self-supervised representation learning: generating effective and data-adaptive augmentations for both vision and non-vision (vector-based) domains where domain-specific heuristic transforms are unavailable.

Extensive empirical evaluations are conducted across multiple tabular/vector benchmarks (HAR, Reuters, Epsilon, MSLR-WEB30K) and vision datasets (CIFAR-10/100, STL-10, ImageNet) across several base contrastive methods (SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, SimSiam, DINO).

Visualizations of the learned Gaussian variance maps show an interesting phenomenon where the noise generator learns to allocate larger variance to background regions and lower variance to foreground objects.
weaknesses: Contrived and tautological theoretical formulation: The core theoretical contribution introduces an auxiliary 1D Gaussian random variable $\alpha | x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \exp(\ell(x; \theta)))$. Because the differential entropy of this Gaussian is strictly monotonic with respect to $\ell(x; \theta)$ ($H(\alpha) = \frac{1}{2}\ell(x; \theta) + \text{const}$), defining 'task entropy' this way merely dresses up the standard contrastive loss inside Gaussian entropy. Deriving that maximizing mutual information recovers the contrastive loss under a Dirac delta assumption is completely circular and provides little genuine information-theoretic insight.

Fundamental optimization flaw and hidden heuristic regularizer: In standard contrastive learning, positive views must be non-trivial to prevent shortcut learning. If the noise generator $f_\psi$ is trained to minimize the contrastive loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{PiNDA}}$ (Eq. 17), the optimal generator trivially collapses to generating zero noise (identity mapping), making positive pairs identical and contrastive loss minimal. To prevent this collapse, the authors introduce an ad-hoc penalty term in Appendix B.4 ('the multiplicative inverse of the average norm of the $\pi$-noises'), which is completely absent from Eq. 17 and the main theoretical narrative. Relying on an unanalyzed, heuristic norm penalty undermines the claimed theoretical foundation.

Substantial computational overhead for marginal performance gains: Generating noise requires an entire second neural network (e.g., a full ResNet-18 or ResNet-50). As reported in Table 6 and Table 9, this roughly doubles the training time, FLOPs, and memory consumption. However, the performance gains over standard baselines on standard vision benchmarks are often negligible or within error margins (e.g., in Table 3 for CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, BYOL achieves $62.21\% \pm 1.00$ baseline vs. $62.74\% \pm 0.57$ with PiNDA; SimSiam achieves $66.29\% \pm 0.16$ baseline vs. $66.39\% \pm 0.56$ with PiNDA; in Table 5 on ImageNet, BYOL gains only +0.20% and SimSiam gains only +0.23%).

Writing, presentation, and unfinished artifacts: The manuscript contains empty URL placeholders for code in both the Abstract and Section 4.2 ('Our code is available at .'). Additionally, there are numerous grammatical errors and colloquial expressions throughout the text (e.g., 'we scientifically investigate', 'a a monotonically increasing function', 'simultaneously learn $\theta$ during finding the $\pi$-noise', 'differ the background from target').

strengths: Exploring automated, learnable data augmentation methods that can generalize beyond computer vision to modalities where domain-specific heuristic transformations are unavailable (e.g., tabular or generic vector data) is an important and relevant problem.

The paper evaluates the proposed approach across multiple data modalities, including non-vision tabular/text benchmarks (HAR, Reuters, Epsilon, MSLR-WEB30K) and vision datasets (CIFAR, STL-10, ImageNet).

The paper includes practical ablation studies, such as analyzing the effect of generator architectures, comparing diagonal Gaussian vs. uniform noise, and profiling computational costs (FLOPs, wall-clock time, and GPU memory in Tables 6, 9, and 10).
weaknesses: Theoretical construction is artificial and lacks foundational justification: The definition of 'task entropy' H(T) in Eq. (6)–(8) relies on defining an ad-hoc auxiliary 1D Gaussian random variable whose inverse variance is artificially set to exp(-loss). This construction is manufactured solely so that the differential entropy of the Gaussian reproduces the contrastive loss function. It does not reflect an intrinsic information-theoretic property of the task or data distribution, making the theoretical connection to mutual information largely superficial.

Objective collapse and hidden heuristic penalty: In Eq. (17), the framework optimizes the generator ψ to directly minimize the contrastive loss L_PiNDA. However, minimizing contrastive loss with respect to positive pair perturbations naturally drives the noise toward zero (i.e., trivial perturbations Σ -> 0 that do not distort the view). As admitted in Appendix B.4, the authors had to introduce an ad-hoc penalty term ('the multiplicative inverse of the average norm of the π-noises') to prevent the learned noise from collapsing to zero. This crucial regularization is absent from the theoretical formulation in Section 3, demonstrating that the information-theoretic formulation in Eq. (14)–(17) is ill-posed on its own.

The claim that predefined data augmentations are 'point estimation of π-noise' is trivial: Describing fixed augmentations as a Dirac delta distribution p(ε|x) -> δ_ε0(ε) in Eq. (12) is merely re-expressing deterministic transformations in distributional notation; it does not constitute a rigorous proof or meaningful insight into data augmentation.

Marginal empirical gains despite substantial computational overhead: On vision benchmarks where standard augmentations are available, the improvements over base contrastive methods are very small (e.g., in Table 3 on CIFAR-10, SimCLR SR improves from 91.98% to 92.25%, BYOL SR from 92.29% to 92.48%, SimSiam SR from 90.73% to 90.85%; on ImageNet in Table 5, BYOL improves from 56.37% to 56.57%, SimSiam from 56.55% to 56.78%). Meanwhile, training an additional deep neural network as a generator (e.g., ResNet-18) roughly doubles training time and adds significant GPU memory overhead (Table 9).

Missing comparisons with established tabular/vector self-supervised methods: For non-vision benchmarks, the paper only compares with SimCL, Random Noise, and CLAE. Standard and effective self-supervised tabular representation learning methods that use corruption/reconstruction or embeddings augmentations (such as SCARF or VIME) are omitted.
